  1                   REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF KAYLYNNE PHILLIPS
 2                          I.   POSITION AND QUALIFICATIONS

 3   Q.   PLEASE STATE YOUR NAME AND BUSINESS ADDRESS.

 4   A.   My name is KayLynne Phillips. I hold the title of Director, Environmental at Oncor

 5        Electric Delivery Company LLC ("Oncor"). My business address is 2471 S. Dallas

 6        Avenue, Lancaster, TX 75146.

 7   Q.   PLEASE DESCRIBE YOUR PROFESSIONAL QUALIFICATIONS.

 8   A.   I hold a Bachelor's degree in Environmental Studies from Baylor University and a

 9        Master's degree in Sustainability and Development from Southern Methodist

10        University. I also hold a professional certificate in Air Quality Engineering. I began

11        working for Oncor in 2009 as a Mickey Leland Environmental Intern before taking

12        a full-time position as an Environmental Specialist in 2010. Since then, I have held

13        various positions at Oncor, including Field Environmental Specialist, Waste

14        Operations Manager, and Senior Manager of Strategic Sourcing and Procurement.

15        I took on my current role as Director of Oncor's Environmental group in May 2024.

16               In my time at Oncor I have been responsible for environmental permitting

17        and compliance including applying for and receiving permits from the Texas

18        Commission on Environmental Quality ("TCEQ"), the United States Fish and

19        Wildlife Service ("USFWS"), the United States Army Corps of Engineers

20        ("USACE"), the Environmental Protection Agency ("EPA'), and the Texas

21        Historical Commission ("THC"). My responsibilities with respect to the proposed

22        Bell County East Switch - Big Hill Substation 765 kilovolt ("kV") transmission line

23        project ("Proposed Transmission        Line   Project" or "Project") will include
     SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349                                         Phillips - Rebuttal
     PUC Docket No. 59475                                               Oncor & LCRA TSC
                                                     Bell County East - Big Hill 765 kV CCN
                                               -2-
  1        environmental permitting for threatened or endangered species, storm water,

 2        cultural resources, and USACE permits as needed.            My educational and

 3        professional qualifications are more fully presented in the attached Exhibit KP-R-

 4        1.
 5   Q.   HAVE YOU EVER SUBMITTED TESTIMONY BEFORE THE PUBLIC UTILITY

 6        COMMISSION OF TEXAS ("COMMISSION")?

 7   A.   Yes. I submitted testimony in Commission Docket No. 59315.

 8                         Il.   PURPOSE OF REBUTTAL TESTIMONY

 9   Q.   DID YOU FILE DIRECT TESTIMONY IN THIS DOCKET?

10   A.   No, I did not.

11   Q.   WHAT IS THE PURPOSE OF YOUR REBUTTAL TESTIMONY?

12   A.   The purpose of my rebuttal testimony is to testify on behalf of Oncor and LCRA

13        Transmission Services Corporation ("LCRA TSC," and, together with Oncor,

14        "Applicants") in support of their application ("Application") to amend their

15        certificates of convenience and necessity ("CCN") in this proceeding.       More

16        specifically, I respond to certain environmental concerns, recommendations, and

17        other issues raised in intervenor testimony regarding Applicants' post-approval

18        environmental permitting activities, environmental standards, and practices, and

19        the Texas Parks and Wildlife Department ("TPWD") coordination with respect to

20        the Proposed Transmission Line Project.

21   Q.   WAS YOUR REBUTTAL TESTIMONY PREPARED BY YOU OR UNDER YOUR

22        DIRECT SUPERVISION AND CONTROL?

     SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349                                       Phillips - Rebuttal
     PUC Docket No. 59475                                             Oncor & LCRA TSC
                                                   Bell County East - Big Hill 765 kV CCN
                                             -3-
  1   A.   Yes.

 2         Ill.   OVERVIEW OF INTERVENORS' ENVIRONMENTAL CONCERNS

 3   Q.   PLEASE GIVE A BRIEF OVERVIEW OF THE ENVIRONMENTAL CONCERNS

 4        RAISED IN INTERVENOR TESTIMONY.

 5   A.   Hundreds of intervenors filed direct testimony in this docket, many of which

 6        expressed concerns about environmental issues. The specific issues they raised

 7        generally fall into several broad categories, including soils, water resources,

 8        vegetation, wildlife, and cultural resources. I address specific issues raised within

 9        each category below.      First, however, I describe Applicants' philosophy for

10        complying with the various environmental statutes, regulations, and permit

11        requirements that govern Applicants' construction of new transmission line

12        projects.   Understanding Applicants' obligations in this regard will help to

13        appropriately frame the intervenors' environmental concerns.

14   Q.   DO      APPLICANTS      COMPLY       WITH     ENVIRONMENTAL           LAWS     AND

15        REGULATIONS AND COORDINATE WITH REGULATORY AUTHORITIES

16        WHEN CONSTRUCTING A NEW TRANSMISSION LINE?

17   A.   Yes. Applicants have a duty to comply with all applicable environmental laws and

18        regulations and take this responsibility very seriously. Applicants operate under

19        various state and federal environmental permits that describe actions Applicants

20        must take under specified conditions to minimize environmental impacts of

21        transmission line construction, operation, and maintenance to the extent feasible.

22        Moreover, as part of the Commission's standard ordering language in CCN

     SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349                                        Phillips - Rebuttal
     PUC Docket No. 59475                                              Oncor & LCRA TSC
                                                    Bell County East - Big Hill 765 kV CCN
                                              -4-
  1        proceedings, the Commission specifically orders Applicants and other electric

 2        utilities to comply with applicable environmental laws and coordinate certain

 3        activities with appropriate agencies, as necessary, during construction of a new

 4        transmission line.

 5   Q.   ARE YOU INVOLVED IN THE ENVIRONMENTAL PERMITTING EFFORTS

 6        THAT APPLICANTS WILL UNDERTAKE TO CONSTRUCT THE PROPOSED

 7        TRANSMISSION LINE?

 8   A.   Yes. As the Director of Oncor's Environmental group, and in my previous positions

 9        with Oncor, I have played a role in regulatory permitting, notification, and

10        compliance for many projects.           Oncor's    Environmental group performs

11        environmental permitting, environmental regulatory agency coordination, and

12        project-specific environmental compliance related to the construction of new

13        transmission lines. I understand that LCRA TSC's environmental group performs

14        the same functions. Applicants take regulatory compliance very seriously and

15        have established standards and practices to ensure compliance with applicable

16        laws, regulations, and permit requirements. If Applicants identify that they have

17        failed to comply with any of these, it is Applicants' standard practice to self-report

18        the violation to the appropriate regulatory authority and mitigate the non-

19        compliance where feasible.

20   Q.   PLEASE      DESCRIBE        APPLICANTS'        ENVIRONMENTAL           PERMITTING

21        ACTIVITIES WHEN CONSTRUCTING A NEW TRANSMISSION LINE.




     SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349                                         Phillips - Rebuttal
     PUC Docket No. 59475                                               Oncor & LCRA TSC
                                                     Bell County East - Big Hill 765 kV CCN
                                               -5-
  1   A.   Generally, once the Commission approves a route for a new transmission line,

 2        qualified experts from Applicants' environmental groups and/or third-party

 3        consultants will conduct a field assessment of the entire length of the right-of-way

 4        ("ROW') for various conditions that might trigger regulatory or permit requirements.

 5        These include the presence of threatened and endangered species, migratory

 6        birds, and critical and/or suitable habitat; navigable waters and potential wetlands;

 7        and historical or cultural resources, among others. Preliminary siting of controls to

 8        manage storm water discharge, runoff, and erosion are identified during this

 9        process. As a result of these assessments, the Applicants' environmental groups

10        identify which permits are necessary, obtain all required environmental permits,

11        and facilitate compliance with the applicable legal and regulatory requirements and

12        permit conditions during construction and operation of the transmission line.

13        Applicants have implemented these processes successfully over many years and

14        hundreds of transmission line projects.

15   Q.   WHY HAVEN'T APPLICANTS ALREADY PERFORMED THAT LEVEL OF

16        DETAILED ENVIRONMENTAL FIELD ASSESSMENTS?

17   A.   The work described in the Environmental Assessment and Alternative Route

18        Analysis for the Proposed Bell County East Switch - Big Hill Substation 765 kV

19        Transmission Line Project in Bell, Burnet, Concho, Coryell, Lampasas, Llano,

20        Mason, McCulloch, Menard, Milam, Mills, San Saba, Schleicher, Tom Green, and

21        Williamson Counties, Texas (" Environmental Assessment and Alternative Route

22        Analysis"), provides sufficient detail for the Commission to effectively differentiate

     SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349                                         Phillips - Rebuttal
     PUC Docket No. 59475                                               Oncor & LCRA TSC
                                                     Bell County East - Big Hill 765 kV CCN
                                               -6-
  1        the aspects of all 122 alternative routes included in the Application, ultimately

 2        providing them with enough information to make an informed decision on a final

 3        route. The Commission has not yet approved a route, and it would not be practical

 4        to conduct detailed surveys of 122 alternative routes ranging in length from

 5        approximately 214-244 miles. Further, before the Application is filed, Applicants

 6        do not have right-of-entry to private properties to perform detailed field

 7        assessments.          Even if Applicants could survey every property that would

 8        potentially be crossed in advance of the filing, doing so would dramatically increase

 9        the time and expense required to prepare a CCN application and be unnecessarily

10        intrusive to landowners. The Commission's final order will ensure that Applicants

11        have the rights necessary to perform detailed field assessments of the approved

12        route efficiently and cost-effectively.     It is not practical nor is it necessary to

13        undertake a comprehensive biological assessment of an entire study area before

14        a final order identifying a route is issued by the Commission.

16   Q.   WHAT IS THE PURPOSE OF THIS SECTION OF YOUR REBUTTAL

17        TESTIMONY?

18   A.   In this     section    of my   rebuttal testimony,    I   discuss specific concerns,

19        recommendations, and other issues raised in intervenor testimony and explain how

20        Applicants will address them during the construction, operation, and maintenance

21        of the Proposed Transmission Line Project.

  1   Q.   IF YOU DO NOT ADDRESS A SPECIFIC CLAIM IN THIS SECTION OF YOUR

 2        REBUTTAL TESTIMONY, DOES THAT INDICATE THAT YOU AGREE WITH

 3        OR CONCEDE THE ISSUES RAISED?

 4   A.   No.    Many intervenor testimonies raised substantially the same environmental

 5        concerns. Therefore, my rebuttal testimony addresses specific issues that were

 6        raised by intervenors and broader categories of intervenor concerns without listing

 7        each individual party who raised them. While I frequently cite specific intervenor

 8        testimonies that articulate those concerns, that does not indicate that my response

 9        does not apply equally to the same or similar concerns voiced by other parties.

10                             A. Soil and Plant Conservation

11   Q.   WERE ANY CONCERNS REGARDING SOIL AND PLANT CONSERVATION

12        COMMONLY EXPRESSED BY INTERVENORS?

13   A.   Yes.     Intervenors expressed various concerns regarding soil disturbance,

14        compaction, and degradation; stormwater runoff, flow patterns, and erosion;

15        protecting native vegetation; and the potential introduction of non-native, invasive

16        vegetation to the ROW.       For example, intervenors Anne Perkins Alex and

17        Christopher Alex (pages 26-27) stated their belief that "[a]ny grading, excavation,

18        road widening, foundation work, or repeated heavy equipment traffic near [water

19        features and drainages] creates a real risk of erosion, sediment movement, and

20        disturbed runoff into the very features that now support the ranch ecologically."

21        Similarly, Crystal Soliz (page 25) testified, "Disruption of the land surface and

22        repeated maintenance activity can affect the natural composition of native grasses

     SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349                                        Phillips - Rebuttal
     PUC Docket No. 59475                                              Oncor & LCRA TSC
                                                    Bell County East - Big Hill 765 kV CCN
                                              -8-
  1        and vegetation, potentially changing drainage patterns and local habitat conditions

 2        over time."

 3   Q.   WHAT ACTIONS WILL APPLICANTS TAKE TO CONSERVE SOILS AND

 4        NATIVE VEGETATION DURING AND AFTER CONSTRUCTION OF THE

 5        PROPOSED TRANSMISSION LINE PROJECT?

 6   A.   During construction, Applicants will undertake soil and plant conservation practices

 7        to protect native vegetation and ensure a successful restoration program for

 8        disturbed areas. When construction activities are complete, Applicants revegetate

 9        the ROW in accordance with TCEQ Texas Pollutant Discharge Elimination System

10        ("TPDES") General Permit No. TXR150000 and the Commission's standard

11        ordering language. Applicants will each need to prepare Storm Water Pollution

12        Prevention Plans ("SWPPP") and submit Notices of Intent to the TCEQ under the

13        TPDES program. Soil erosion prevention and controls and soil compaction are

14        addressed in Applicants' SWPPPs. Oncor uses sediment controls that are

15        referenced in the Integrated Stormwater Management (iSWM) Manual that is

16        maintained by the North Central Texas Council of Governments.           LCRA TSC

17        follows EPA, TCEQ, and/or TxDOT approved stormwater controls. Controls are

18        customized for each project, but some examples include the use of erosion control

19        blankets, turf reinforcement mats, berms, silt fence, and mulching. Compaction will

20        be addressed wherever necessary to facilitate revegetation in accordance with the

21        SWPPP.

22   Q.   WILL APPLICANTS REVEGETATE THE ROW USING NATIVE SPECIES?

     SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349                                        Phillips - Rebuttal
     PUC Docket No. 59475                                              Oncor & LCRA TSC
                                                    Bell County East - Big Hill 765 kV CCN
                                              -9-
  1   A.   Applicants' standard revegetation practices emphasize native species while also

 2        considering Iandowner preferences, wildlife needs, existing land uses, and costs.

 3   Q.   HOW DO APPLICANTS PREVENT INVASIVE SPECIES FROM BEING

 4        INTRODUCED TO THE ROW?

 5   A.   Applicants direct their Vegetation Management ("VM") contractors to make every

 6        effort to keep vehicles and equipment clean in order to prevent the inadvertent

 7        introduction of invasive species to the ROW.

 8   Q.   A FEW INTERVENORS, INCLUDING TIMOTHY HEFNER (PAGE 15) AND

 9        WENDY & SHIRLEY FLEMING (PAGE 21), VOICE CONCERNS ABOUT

10        POTENTIAL IMPACTS OF ROW CLEARING ON POLLINATORS.                              DO

11        APPLICANTS CONSIDER THE NEEDS OF POLLINATOR SPECIES DURING

12        ROW RESTORATION?

13   A.   Applicants will consider Iandowner preferences as part of their restoration and

14        revegetation efforts, including revegetation with pollinator friendly flora.   The

15        Applicants use Integrated Vegetation Management ("IVM") principles, discussed

16        in further detail below, which have been shown to increase habitat diversity and

17        provide benefits for pollinator species.

18   Q.   SEVERAL INTERVENORS, INCLUDING KAREN SMITH HUBBARD ON

19        BEHALF OF JEROME AND GAYLYNN SNEED (PAGE 22), RAISE CONCERNS

20        ABOUT      APPLICANTS'         VEGETATION         MANAGEMENT          PRACTICES,

21        PARTICULARLY PESTICIDE             USE AND THEIR IMPACT TO                NEARBY




     SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349                                         Phillips - Rebuttal
     PUC Docket No. 59475                                               Oncor & LCRA TSC
                                                     Bell County East - Big Hill 765 kV CCN
                                              -10-
  1        WATERWAYS. HOW DO APPLICANTS MANAGE VEGETATION IN THE ROW

 2        AFTER CONSTRUCTION AND ROW RESTORATION ARE COMPLETE?

 3   A.   After construction and ROW restoration are complete, Applicants employ IVM

 4        principles. IVM is the process of promoting compatible, stable, low-growing plant

 5        communities that will resist the encroachment of trees by using environmentally

 6        sound and cost-effective control methods.          IVM can create early successional

 7        habitats that are valuable for wildlife, native species, and pollinators while allowing

 8        safe and reliable power delivery.

 9               Herbicides used by Applicants are pre-blended as concentrates or ready to

10        use mixes in order to ensure proper ratios. All products must be labeled, approved,

11        and suitable for the site of application. The label is the law; herbicides must be

12        used according to EPA-approved label directions. Only products labeled for

13        Industrial/ROWVM from select manufacturers are approved for use by Applicants'

14        respective environmental departments.

15               Applicants use licensed herbicide applicators that are required to exercise

16        extreme care to avoid affecting non-targeted vegetation or animal life and must

17        use selective application methods that minimize impacts on compatible vegetation.

18        Applicants will follow their respective TPDES General Permits from the TCEQ for

19        aquatic applications.

20   Q.   SEVERAL INTERVENORS EXPRESS CONCERNS ABOUT PERMANENT

21        DAMAGE TO OAK TREES DUE TO ROOTS BEING EXPOSED TO OAK WILT.

22        HOW DO YOU RESPOND TO THIS CONCERN?

     SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349                                            Phillips - Rebuttal
     PUC Docket No. 59475                                                  Oncor & LCRA TSC
                                                        Bell County East - Big Hill 765 kV CCN
                                               - 11 -
  1   A.   Root system damage or disturbance of oak trees does not increase the spread of

 2        oak wilt. Oak wilt can only be spread from open "wounds" in live wood or

 3        subsurface roots or transmitted from one already infected tree to a non-infected

 4        tree via their root systems. All oak trees located within the ROW will be removed,

 5        as that species is incompatible with the safe, reliable operation of the proposed

 6        transmission line. Clearing will be done with above-ground methods, keeping the

 7        root systems intact.   VM contractors will take precautions in accordance with

 8        American National Standards Institute ("ANSI") performance standard A300 to

 9        avoid stripping or tearing bark and excessive wounding. VM contractors will also

10        implement control methods, as appropriate, including in counties where oak wilt

11        centers have been identified. When using mechanical control methods, cuts will

12        be made as close to the main stem as practicable, outside the branch bark ridge

13        and branch collar.

15   Q.   A NUMBER OF PARTIES, INCLUDING JASON AARON HOWTON (PAGES 10-

16        12), RONALD L. BOULTINGHOUSE (PAGE 18), AND RYAN HOPKINS ON

17        BEHALF OF THE G6 LANDOWNERS LEGAL FUND LLC (PAGE 33) EXPRESS

21   A.   As Applicants' witness Corin Cooley describes in her rebuttal testimony, Applicants

22        typically span surface water features where possible.       Also, Applicants' pre-

  1   Q.   WHAT IS YOUR RESPONSE TO INTERVENOR CONCERNS WITH IMPACTS

 2        TO WATER RESOURCES AS A RESULT OF POTENTIAL HERBICIDE

 3        RUNOFF?
 4   A.   Applicants'   herbicide programs are low volume programs meaning that

 5        applications are low volume, low pressure (basal or stump treatments/selective,

 6        directly to the target vegetation) and that Applicants only apply herbicides to

 7        targeted vegetation that is within 5% or less of the total area of a Iandowner's

 8        property within the ROW. (If Applicants target an area for high volume application,

 9        then Applicants will notify and seek documented permission from the Iandowner

10        prior to performing the application.) Applicants' typical herbicide applications are

11        spot treatments applied via hand pump around the base of the transmission line

12        structure and/or at ROW gate/fence crossings.

13               Regarding concerns related to potential impacts on water bodies,

14        Applicants' licensed herbicide applicators apply herbicides in accordance with the

15        manufacturer's recommendations. As noted above, Applicants' herbicide use is

16        part of their IVM plans. The plans include using herbicides to selectively eliminate

17        certain trees that have the potential to grow into the danger zone of a transmission

18        line, while preserving and cultivating more desirable native grasses, shrubs, and

19        even trees that will never potentially impact the operation of the transmission

20        system.

  1   Q.   MANY        INTERVENORS        EXPRESS      CONCERNS       ABOUT      IMPACTS      TO

 2        WILDLIFE.       HOW DO APPLICANTS AVOID IMPACTS TO WILDLIFE

 3        ENCOUNTERED ALONG THE APPROVED ROUTE?

 4   A.   As Applicants' witness Mr. Russell Marusak discusses in more detail in his rebuttal

 5        testimony, before filing the CCN Application, Applicants attempted to avoid impacts

 6        to wildlife by proposing routing alternatives that minimize distances through

 7        potential habitat for listed species, in particular preserves or parks containing these

 8        species, and minimizing impacts by paralleling existing compatible ROWs, where

 9        feasible.    Applicants, Halff Associates, Inc. ("Halff'), and Kimley-Horn and

10        Associates, Inc. ("Kimley-Horn") consulted with regulatory agencies, performed

11        desktop and reconnaissance surveys of the study area, modeled potential habitat

12        that may be encountered on each route, assessed potential impacts, and

13        determined BMPs to avoid or minimize adverse impacts.

14               As discussed in the Environmental Assessment and Alternative Route

15        Analysis, the TPWD maintains the Texas Natural Diversity Database ("TXNDD")

16        to track known occurrences of threatened, endangered, and otherwise rare plant

17        and animal species throughout Texas. The TXNDD provides information about

18        sensitive habitats and areas managed to achieve species diversity or provide

19        quality habitat for wildlife species. Applicants consult the TXNDD as part of its

20        routing and pre-construction processes. The direct testimony of Applicants'

21        witness Mr. Russell Marusak describes the route-development process and TPWD

22        consultation in more detail.

 4        DESCRIBE CONCERNS ABOUT POTENTIAL IMPACTS TO THE GOLDEN-

18   A.   As they have always done in the past, Applicants intend to comply with all
